title: Fifteen voices
hook: Kabir, Farid, Namdev, Ravidas, Trilochan, Beni, Dhanna, Sain, Pipa, Sadhna, Ramanand, Parmanand, Surdas, Jaidev and Bhikhan

segments.voice: Yesterday the janamsakhi closed, and your line was my favorite sakhi. Which one did you choose, and did it surprise you? Today a new stretch of the road begins. Day seven hundred forty-seven.

Kabir. Farid. Namdev. Ravidas. Trilochan. Beni. Dhanna. Sain. Pipa. Sadhna. Ramanand. Parmanand. Surdas. Jaidev. Bhikhan. Not one of those names belongs to a Sikh Guru. Some were Hindu devotees, some came from Muslim families, and by their own words several worked with their hands: a weaver, a man who carried dead cattle, a cloth printer. And yet their hymns sit inside the Guru Granth Sahib, the book Sikhs bow to as their living Guru. For the next stretch of days we meet these singers one by one. Today, all of them at once.
screen: `FIFTEEN NAMES, NO GURU AMONG THEM.` → `WEAVERS, PRINTERS, DEVOTEES.` → `INSIDE THE GURU'S OWN BOOK.`

segments.voice: Sikhs call them the bhagats, the devotees. Tradition says that when Guru Arjan gathered the hymns that became the Granth, he set the words of these saints beside the words of the Gurus. Where their hymns appear, they come at the end of a raag's section, after the Gurus' own. And there they are, under the same musical headings, read in the same voice by the same granthi, bowed to the same way. There's a hymn in Raag Asa, at the start of Bhagat Dhanna's hymns, that is almost a roll call. It tells how Namdev, a calico printer worth half a copper coin, became worth a fortune. How Kabir left his loom for love of the Lord's feet. How Ravidas, who carried dead cattle, let go of the world's pull. How Sain, the barber, became a devotee. And Dhanna, a farmer, hears all this and gets up to give his own life to devotion. Look at that list. It doesn't open with a king or a priest. It opens with working people, named by their trades. The bhagat hymns sign themselves, too. Listen and you'll hear Kahu Kabir, says Kabir, or Kahi Ravidas, says Ravidas, near the end. The voices stay distinct. Their accents differ, their languages differ, some lines sound like a village and some like a court. And yet in the Sikh telling there isn't a front section for the Gurus and a back shelf for guests. The whole book together is the Guru. That's today's line: fifteen voices, one guru.
screen: `THE BHAGATS: THE DEVOTEES.` · `AT THE END OF A RAAG.` · `A ROLL CALL OF WORKING PEOPLE.` · `THE HYMNS SIGN THEIR NAMES.` · then, large: `FIFTEEN VOICES, ONE GURU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say three names slowly. Settle, and let your breath find its own pace. Pick any three of the fifteen. Kabir, Farid, Ravidas, or any that catch your ear. Say the first one, quietly or in your head, and let it ring out like a bell. Wait. Then the second. Then the third. Don't try to know anything about them yet. Just let each name be a person who once sang. If you pray, you can follow the three names with Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Fifteen voices. The bhagats, saints from many castes and backgrounds, whose hymns sit inside the Guru Granth Sahib beside the Gurus' own.
Your line: fifteen voices, one guru. Today, notice one voice you usually skip past, a coworker, a neighbor, a cousin, and hear it out to the end. Day seven hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: In gurdwaras the hymns of the bhagats are sung in kirtan and read in the Guru Granth Sahib with the same honor as the Gurus' hymns, and the bhagat hymns carry their singers' names.

fork.setup: you're gathering a holy book for a community. you have hymns from saints who were never part of it: a weaver, a cobbler, a farmer, a Sufi. what do you do with them?
options: leave them out; the book is for our own teachers.
print them in a separate appendix.
set them in the book, same music, same honor.
fork.reveal: tradition says Guru Arjan set them inside, under the same raags, and Sikhs bow to the whole book as the Guru.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: a devotee. the singers of these hymns are called the bhagats.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Sikh scripture holds only the Sikh Gurus' words.
what it means: bhagats from many castes and backgrounds sing inside it too, and the whole book is the Guru.
what a scholar hears: a bhagat hymn keeps its singer's signature line, so the voices stay distinct inside one book.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Raag Asa, Ang 487–488 (the hymn opening Bhagat Dhanna's section: Namdev, Kabir, Ravidas, Sain, Dhanna)
Guru Granth Sahib: arrangement of bhagat bani at the end of each raag

notes: The count 'fifteen' comes from the index title and outline; the Granth itself does not state it. Counts vary depending on whether the bhatts, Satta and Balwand, and Baba Sundar are grouped with the bhagats. Confirm how this path wants to frame the number.

The Raag Asa hymn at Ang 487–488 opening Dhanna's section is attributed by many editions to Guru Arjan (Mahalla 5) rather than Dhanna; the script says only that it sits 'at the start of Bhagat Dhanna's hymns'. Confirm Ang and phrasing ('half a shell', 'worth a fortune', 'carried dead cattle').
Compilation by Guru Arjan attributed to tradition; no date given.
'Some were Hindu devotees, some came from Muslim families' kept general; confirm acceptable (Farid, Bhikhan; Kabir's background is taught tomorrow).
Signature lines 'Kahu Kabir' / 'Kahi Ravidas' given as transliterations, not quotations; confirm forms.
Day 746 script not on disk at writing; review written from the index (word 'The sakhis close', carry 'my favorite sakhi'). Start of Block C (Bhagats of the Granth).

Editor: softened 'at the end of each raag' (not every raag has bhagat bani) and 'each bhagat hymn signs itself' to non-universal wording in teach, screen, myth, trapdoor and howItsDone; cut stock line 'here's the part that stays with people'.
Audit: 'worth half a shell' corrected to 'half a copper coin' (the hymn's aadh daam is half a dam, a copper coin, not a cowrie shell); moved 'that's today's line' so it follows the line it names.
